messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, December 11, 2014 12:29:48 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > I am evolving into the opinion that I should be focusing on parameters for convergence monitoring.
>
> As Michael pointed out, every function of the parameters should also converge.
> I don't know if there's some way to estimate a total "n_eff".  I now don't know
> what to make of runs where one parameter gets n_eff=100 and another n_eff=1000.

This is true (marginally), but if the chain has converged (jointly), then every function of the things in the parameters block will converge (marginally). The difficulty for multivariate convergence monitoring is that if some unknown has a much bigger scale, then it tends to dominate any distance-based calculation. If it were merely a rescaling, then we would be okay, but if something in generated quantities is like the exp() of something in parameters, then it becomes overly sensitive to the less important thing. Since we are telling people that they need to have reasonable scales on the things in the parameters block, then I think we should at least have the option to do the joint convergence monitoring on the parameters only.

Ben

hi folks,

there seems to be some confusion about
which algorithm we have implemented in
the bbvb branch, what shape its in, and
where we'd like to take it.

attached is our submission to the nips
2014 prob prog workshop. this describes
the state of the art of what lives in the
bbvb branch. it is a simple yet novel
algorithm.

note that this is not standard variational
bayes. the core differences are:

+ gaussian variational approximation
in unconstrained parameter space

+ gradient-based algorithm. *not*
coordinate ascent.

+ stochastic optimize. *not* the same
as stochastic variational inference (SVI)
where data is subsampled.

please feel free to peruse and comment.

our next goals are to test the current
code on more complicated models and
get started on implementing SVI. this
will allow stan to address massive datasets,
which piqued many peoples interest
at nips 2014.

cheers,
alp

messages.subject: CDF and CCDF exceptions or 0/1 returns?
messages.subject_clean: CDF and CCDF exceptions or 0/1 returns?
messages.body_plain:
Daniel, Rob and I discussed this issue and concluded that what we want
is to have CDFs and CCDFs throw exceptions if there are inputs outside
of support of the corresponding density.

Example 1:  closed support interval

   uniform_cdf(y, L, U);

   support is [L,U]

   if y not in [L,U] throw an exception

Example 2:  open support interval

   lognormal_cdf(y, mu, sigma);

   support is (0,inf)

   if y not in (0,inf), throw an exception (that is, throw on 0 or +inf)

Is this OK with everyone?

The alternative is obviously to have CDFs return 0 for y below support and
1 for y above support.  We thought having the exceptions would help users diagnose
problems more easily.

- Bob

messages.subject: Performance Regression
messages.body_plain:
I just wanted to mention some performance regression that’s taken place
since 2.4.0, mostly due to all of the NaN checking that was added.

First-order gradients have gradually slowed by about 5% from a variety
of contributions (the new memory pattern, nested autodiff, NaN checking,
etc).  Each commit yields a pretty marginal change in performance and
only the aggregate performance manifests in a noticeable slowdown,
at least as far as I can tell.

Higher-order derivatives took a huge hit from the introduction of fvar
NaN checks in https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/commit/2c4cc3ee5b78fa7cee563a1d9faf569b17c8f447,
slowing down by over 67%.  There is no immediate solution to this
slow down without removing the NaN checks — in Nomad I avoided
this by having the checks templated and readily turned off by the user
when speed is a concern.
